hero.headline: US diesel prices reach all-time high as Iran conflict disrupts fuel supply
hero.teaser: Diesel prices across the United States have climbed to unprecedented levels, exceeding the previous record reached in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The national average
hero.body:
Diesel prices across the United States have climbed to unprecedented levels, exceeding the previous record reached in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The national average for diesel now stands at $5.85 per gallon, driven by supply disruptions stemming from the conflict that began in late February.

The price surge reflects broader increases in wholesale oil markets since the Iran conflict started. The war has interrupted global fuel supply chains, particularly affecting petroleum shipments from the Middle East. The combination of Iran's significance to global energy markets and ongoing constraints from the Ukraine situation has created mounting pressure on diesel availability worldwide.

The economic ripple effects extend far beyond gas stations. Diesel fuels the majority of commercial trucks, freight trains, farm equipment, and construction machinery throughout the country. Transportation and logistics companies facing higher fuel costs typically transfer these expenses to consumers through increased prices for goods and services.

Farmers have been hit especially hard. Diesel is essential for operating tractors, harvesters, and irrigation systems, making fuel cost increases directly threaten agricultural profitability. Both American and British farmers have reported experiencing what observers describe as astronomical fuel price increases, caught between dual pressures from conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

The price increases add to inflationary concerns throughout the broader economy. As policymakers consider interest rate decisions, the fuel cost surge affects production and distribution across multiple sectors. Food production, retail delivery, and countless other industries depend on transportation, meaning diesel prices significantly influence the final costs consumers pay for everyday goods.

The global oil market dynamics underscore the far-reaching consequences of regional conflicts. Supply disruptions from the strait of Hormuz have removed substantial quantities of oil from international markets, creating cascading price effects in fuel markets worldwide. While some disruptions have been partially offset through alternative routes and emergency reserves, the underlying supply constraints continue to pressure prices upward.

The situation highlights how regional instability can quickly translate into economic consequences for households and businesses thousands of miles away. For consumers, the diesel spike represents higher costs for transported goods and services. For industries dependent on fuel-intensive operations, it threatens margins and competitiveness. For farmers managing tight profit margins, surging diesel costs can determine whether operations remain viable.

As the Iran conflict continues, market participants are closely monitoring developments that could either ease or intensify the current supply crisis. The resolution of regional tensions remains a crucial factor in determining whether diesel prices will stabilize at current elevated levels or climb further, with significant implications for inflation and economic growth in the months ahead.

cards.headline: Trump envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv this weekend as U.S. pushes new peace proposal
cards.teaser: U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend as part of efforts to broker a peace deal in the war that began with Russia's invasi
cards.body:
U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend as part of efforts to broker a peace deal in the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed he will meet the envoys on Sunday, following their talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday. President Donald Trump told reporters the envoys are bringing a proposal to end the war, though a gulf remains between the two sides.

Witkoff and Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, have visited Russia multiple times but this will be their first trip to Ukraine since leading the U.S. peace effort. Zelensky said he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to reciprocate for Ukraine. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to confirm the visit but said the government would inform reporters when such contacts take place.

Putin told an international economic forum on Thursday that there are chances a peace deal could be reached, saying Moscow and Kyiv must first agree between themselves. He showed no sign of backing down from demands that include additional territorial concessions from Ukraine. Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly rejected Putin's terms, calling them tantamount to capitulation.

Earlier on Friday, Zelensky said a Russian drone struck the Kyiv office of Oleksandr Poklad, head of the SBU security service. Poklad appeared unharmed. Zelensky said he ordered Poklad to respond adequately to the attack. Russia currently controls about 20 percent of Ukrainian territory.

cards.headline: US military strikes three Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attacks on American warships
cards.teaser: The US military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday in retaliation for attacks on American warships, escalating a six-month conflict that has disrupted global energy suppl
cards.body:
The US military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday in retaliation for attacks on American warships, escalating a six-month conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies. US Central Command said it permanently disabled two tankers, including one near Kharg Island, and completely destroyed a third in the Gulf of Oman. The attacks came after Centcom said it evaded multiple attacks from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps earlier in the day targeting a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American troops were harmed.

Iran's state media confirmed the strikes and said Tehran launched retaliatory attacks on six vessels in the region, including three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz traveling what Iran called an unauthorized route. Iranian state outlet Irib reported no casualties in the attack near Kharg Island, which hosts Iran's main oil export terminal and handles roughly 90 percent of the country's crude oil. Crews from the two tankers struck in the Gulf of Oman reached shore in lifeboats, according to Irib.

Centcom claimed the three Iranian tankers were part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network funding the IRGC and its regional proxies. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on social media hours before Iran's retaliation that if Iran shoots at US ships, the military will destroy their oil tankers. The strikes marked the latest escalation in fighting that resumed last week after a period of relative calm.

The conflict has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz since fighting began in February, squeezing a waterway that previously carried about 20 percent of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. The disruption has raised energy prices globally, with the average US diesel price reaching $5.85 per gallon on Friday compared to $3.71 a year earlier. A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran expired last month with little sign of a diplomatic settlement ahead of US midterm elections in November.

cards.headline: Oil Prices Jump to $90 a Barrel After U.S. and Iran Exchange Attacks
cards.teaser: Crude oil prices surged past $90 a barrel after a two-month window for negotiations between the United States and Iran expired without progress, triggering renewed military exchang
cards.body:
Crude oil prices surged past $90 a barrel after a two-month window for negotiations between the United States and Iran expired without progress, triggering renewed military exchanges and rattling global energy markets.

Brent crude rose above $90 for the first time since late July, reaching $91.63 by Tuesday morning. The escalation came after Iran signaled it would adopt a more aggressive military stance if talks failed, while President Donald Trump demanded Tehran "put up the white flag of surrender" in a Fox News interview. Trump also threatened to bomb Oman if it interfered with his efforts to resolve the conflict, marking the second time he has directed such a threat at the U.S. strategic partner.

The prospect of expanded conflict alarmed energy analysts watching the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil shipments. Roughly a quarter of all seaborne oil normally passes through the waterway. An Iranian military official warned that vessels attempting transit would "find several beautiful holes in their hulls," and a cargo ship was attacked while traveling through the strait early Tuesday.

Ship traffic through the strait plummeted as tensions mounted. Just six cargo vessels transited on Monday, according to ship tracking company Kpler, compared to only five combined on Saturday and Sunday. Angeline Ong, a senior technical analyst at IG, suggested Trump's threat against Oman could mark a turning point for oil markets. "If Muscat pulls back from talks with Tehran, the diplomatic route to restoring normal flows through Hormuz narrows considerably," Ong said, adding that investors might shift from betting on temporary disruption to pricing in prolonged supply problems.

Deutsche Bank analysts interpreted the rising oil prices as evidence that investors were preparing for an extended closure of the strait. The economic consequences rippled across markets. U.S. gasoline prices remained elevated at 37 percent higher than before the conflict began, continuing to pressure household budgets and inflation. Bond yields climbed to multi-year highs as investors reassessed growth and inflation expectations.

Trump indicated he was not rushing to end the conflict, telling Fox News he had "no time schedule" and was "not in a hurry" to reach a deal, despite claiming months earlier that resolution was imminent.

Geopolitical strategists warned of compounding risks. Dan Alamariu at Alpine Macro cautioned that escalation through the fall could produce a "double shock" if combined with Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine. He predicted energy market volatility would spike with sustained, intense Middle East conflict, particularly affecting oil and gas prices.

The developments prompted G20 finance officials to convene in the United States for meetings centered on the economic fallout from the Iran conflict.

cards.headline: Trump announces deal for U.S. access to Venezuelan oil reserves
cards.teaser: President Trump says the U.S. has struck an agreement to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil.
cards.body:
President Trump announced Friday that the U.S. has struck a deal to develop Venezuela's oil reserves, with the American government taking a majority stake in the project. Trump characterized the arrangement as beneficial for Americans, pointing to the nation's vast oil deposits.

Energy experts caution against expecting immediate results. Francisco Monaldi, director of the Latin America Energy Program at Rice University, explained that developing Venezuela's reserves requires substantial time and investment, and would not lead to lower gas prices in the near term.

cards.headline: August Jobs Report Shows Strong Hiring, Raising Pressure on Federal Reserve
cards.teaser: U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August, marking an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1 percent, down from its pea
cards.body:
U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August, marking an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1 percent, down from its peak of 4.5 percent in November, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The August hiring represents a rebound from inconsistent job growth in recent months. Job additions have fluctuated significantly, ranging from 214,000 in March to just 21,000 in July. The June and July figures were revised upward following initial releases, with June revised up by 11,000 and July revised up by 44,000 jobs.

Economists had predicted at least 50,000 new jobs would be added in August. The actual figure exceeded those expectations. However, other employment indicators painted a more mixed picture. The payroll firm ADP reported that private companies added just 38,000 jobs in August, marking the lowest monthly total since January. Meanwhile, the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas reported that announced layoffs declined 41 percent compared to the same period last year.

Labor market analysts describe the current employment situation as stalled in a "slow hire, slow fire" state, with neither significant growth nor substantial contractions. A separate BLS report showed job openings and layoffs changed little in July. The number of workers quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting declining worker confidence about finding alternative employment.

The August employment data arrives amid persistent economic pressures facing households. U.S. inflation increased significantly, rising from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July, with a peak of 4.2 percent in May. This marks the highest rate since 2023. Rising prices have compounded frustrations for many Americans even as job gains continue.

The inflation concerns have rippled through financial markets. Yields on U.S. Treasury bonds have risen, signaling investor concerns about long-term economic health. Higher bond yields could push up borrowing costs across mortgages, car loans, and student debt.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh recently stated the central bank remained committed to lowering inflation to its 2 percent target. "We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed," Warsh said. "Otherwise, we have work to do." Economists expect at least one interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve before year's end.

The strong August employment figures complicate political pressures on the central bank. President Trump has publicly urged the Fed to cut rates and threatened to halt trade with countries holding trade deficits if the central bank does not comply. The robust jobs data provides economic justification for the Fed to maintain its current course or pursue rate increases rather than cuts, potentially undermining those pressure campaigns.

cards.headline: Employer Health Costs Expected to Jump 11 Percent in 2027
cards.teaser: A new survey of U.S. employers projects that health care costs will surge by an average of 11 percent in 2027, marking the highest rate of increase in decades. Without significant
cards.body:
A new survey of U.S. employers projects that health care costs will surge by an average of 11 percent in 2027, marking the highest rate of increase in decades. Without significant changes to benefit structures, companies face mounting pressure to control expenses while maintaining competitive coverage for workers.

The anticipated spike reflects the ongoing challenge of health care cost inflation, which has consistently outpaced general price increases across the economy. This year, U.S. inflation cooled to an annual rate of 3.5 percent in June, largely due to energy price declines during a brief ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran. However, subsequent tensions have driven oil prices back up, and broader economic pressures from elevated borrowing costs continue to strain both businesses and households.

The survey indicates that employers will likely face difficult decisions about how to manage the projected increase. Companies may respond by shifting more costs to employees through higher deductibles, increased premiums, or reduced benefit offerings. Some employers may also limit coverage in other ways to offset the substantial rise in health care expenses.

The 11 percent projection significantly exceeds typical annual growth rates seen in recent years and comes as businesses navigate an uncertain economic environment. Many companies have historically absorbed some health care cost increases to remain competitive in attracting and retaining talent, but the scale of this anticipated jump may limit their willingness or ability to do so.

Workers could face the most direct impact through higher out-of-pocket expenses for medical care. Additional survey findings also predicted sharp increases across different measures of health care spending, though specific details varied among the projections.

The findings add another layer of complexity for U.S. businesses already dealing with economic headwinds. Companies operating across industries will need to balance maintaining adequate health benefits for employees against the need to control expenses and protect profit margins. This calculation could reshape workplace health coverage in coming years, potentially leading to widespread changes in how Americans access and pay for medical care.

The projected cost surge underscores the persistent challenge of health care affordability in the United States. As employers grapple with the 11 percent increase, workers may increasingly face trade-offs between comprehensive coverage and out-of-pocket costs. The survey results suggest that without intervention or changes to the broader health care system, both employers and employees will feel significant pressure in 2027.

hero.headline: Egyptian court sentences TV presenter and 11 others to death in drug trafficking case
hero.teaser: Sarah Khalifa and 11 defendants convicted after seizure of more than 750kg of narcotics and raw materials.
hero.body:
An Egyptian court sentenced television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people to death by hanging after convicting them of drug trafficking charges. The defendants were part of a criminal gang that imported ingredients used to make drugs with intent to sell, according to state-owned newspaper al-Ahram. Authorities seized more than 750 kilograms of narcotics and raw materials during the investigation. The defendants also faced charges of possessing illegal firearms and munitions.

Khalifa, 39, is known for hosting the crime program Mission Impossible and has denied the charges. The verdict was announced last month and confirmed after the court obtained a required religious opinion from Egypt's grand mufti. Khalifa told the court last September that she had never seen drugs until she was photographed with them inside anti-narcotics authority offices. The verdict can be appealed.

cards.headline: Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway's King Harald V
cards.teaser: The Prince of Wales will attend the Oslo service Wednesday as European royals gather to honor the modernizing monarch who reigned for 35 years.
cards.body:
Prince William will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway in Oslo on Wednesday, representing his father King Charles, Buckingham Palace announced. Princess Anne will also attend in a personal capacity as godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII. King Harald, who died last month at age 89 after 35 years on the throne, was widely regarded as a modernizing figure who helped reshape the Norwegian monarchy.

Large crowds are expected for the funeral procession and service at Oslo Cathedral, following days of public mourning during which thousands queued to pay respects at the Royal Palace chapel. The service will be attended by widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family, and other European royals. King Haakon assumes his role amid recent scandals in the royal family, including Queen Mette-Marit's public apology for maintaining a friendship with Jeffrey Epstein and the rape conviction of her son from a previous relationship.

cards.headline: Greek air force F-4 Phantom jet crashes at air show near Athens, killing both pilots
cards.teaser: A Greek air force F-4 Phantom jet crashed during an air show at Tanagra air force base north of Athens on Saturday, killing both pilots. The twin-seat aircraft flew into the ground
cards.body:
A Greek air force F-4 Phantom jet crashed during an air show at Tanagra air force base north of Athens on Saturday, killing both pilots. The twin-seat aircraft flew into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver just meters above the surface as thousands of spectators watched during the annual Athens Flying Week event. No civilians were injured.

The jet burst into flames on impact and sent up a large plume of black smoke. Eighty-five firefighters assisted by 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters worked to extinguish the blaze. Video of the crash showed a second ball of fire nearby as the plane broke apart. The bodies of the pilots were later recovered. An eyewitness told ERT, Greece's state broadcaster, that the jet had been airborne for no more than three minutes.

Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the sense of grief was widespread and that his thoughts were with the families of the two pilots. He described the crash as a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greek aviators who remain on constant standby to protect the country's skies. Cyprus Defense Minister Vasilis Palmas expressed sadness at the deaths and said he had called Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias.

Organizers canceled the remainder of Athens Flying Week following the incident and evacuated the area. The Greek air force declared three days of national mourning.

cards.headline: Russia Suspected in Series of Sabotage Incidents Across Europe
cards.teaser: European governments are investigating a widening campaign of sabotage across the continent, with Russia emerging as the primary suspect. Germany has blamed Russia for an attack on
cards.body:
European governments are investigating a widening campaign of sabotage across the continent, with Russia emerging as the primary suspect. Germany has blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport, which fits into a broader pattern of suspicious incidents targeting infrastructure in multiple countries.

The incidents represent what analysts describe as hybrid warfare, employing tactics that stop short of conventional military conflict. Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in Germany. Poland has also faced suspected acts of sabotage, and unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe.

These attacks highlight a significant challenge for European policymakers. Governments are quicker to publicly blame Moscow for the incidents, but critics argue that their limited responses may invite further sabotage. The question of how to impose meaningful costs on Russia for attacks that deliberately fall below the threshold of conventional war remains unresolved.

The campaign reflects heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations since the start of the war in Ukraine. European officials are weighing potential solutions to counter what they characterise as growing hybrid warfare tactics. The United States has urged NATO allies to prepare for potential Russian attacks, reflecting broader concerns about Moscow's intentions.

European governments face a difficult balancing act in responding to the incidents. Officials must work to deter further attacks while avoiding unpredictable consequences that could spiral out of control. The risk of escalation looms over any European response, as miscalculation or unintended consequences could trigger a wider conflict.

The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure across the continent. The ongoing investigations into the Leipzig airport attack and other incidents reflect Europe's efforts to assess defensive postures and develop strategies to counter unconventional threats. These threats operate in a grey zone below armed conflict, making them particularly difficult to address through traditional security responses.

The sabotage campaign has created an unnerving security environment across Europe. Political leaders have expressed alarm about the pattern of incidents, emphasising the need for coordinated responses. However, the challenge of determining appropriate consequences for hybrid warfare tactics remains one of the most pressing security questions facing European nations.

As investigations continue, European governments are working to establish clearer circumstances around individual incidents while developing broader strategies to counter Russia's suspected campaign. The incidents underscore the evolving nature of modern security threats and the difficulty of responding effectively to actions that fall short of traditional military aggression but pose serious risks to critical infrastructure and public safety across the continent.

hero.headline: Casting for next James Bond may conclude by year's end, producer says
hero.teaser: The search for the seventh official 007 has entered final rounds, with auditions under way and an announcement possible within months.
hero.body:
The casting process for the next James Bond actor may produce a decision by the end of this year, according to producer Amy Pascal. Amazon MGM Studios confirmed in May that the search was under way. Entertainment writer Daniel Richtman reported last month that producers are in the final round of casting and may have already found their choice. Names discussed during the process have included Henry Cavill, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Jack Lowden, James Norton, and Paul Mescal, though it remains unclear which actors have formally auditioned.

Only six actors have played Bond in the official film series. The last announcement came in 2005. The next film, known as Bond 26, will be written by Steven Knight and directed by Denis Villeneuve, with a release widely expected in 2028. That would mark the longest gap between Bond films in franchise history, surpassing the six years between Licence to Kill and GoldenEye.

cards.headline: Katie Taylor retires after winning final bout in Dublin
cards.teaser: The Irish boxer won her final professional fight to become undisputed light-welterweight champion, finishing with 26 wins from 27 contests.
cards.body:
Katie Taylor ended her boxing career with a points victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park in Dublin, becoming undisputed light-welterweight champion in front of more than 80,000 fans. The 40-year-old Irish fighter retires with 26 wins from 27 professional contests, Olympic gold, and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions.

Prominent figures in women's boxing praised Taylor's career and legacy. Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called her "one of the best to ever do it," while American fighter Claressa Shields said Taylor deserved to "ride off into the sunset." Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner described Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us." Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew said he had never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms.

cards.headline: Federal judge reinforces order requiring 48-hour notice before work on Trump's proposed Arlington arch
cards.teaser: A district court reinforced its order after the Interior secretary announced plans to break ground within weeks on the controversial 250-foot structure near Arlington National Cemetery.
cards.body:
A federal judge ordered the Trump administration on Friday to provide 48 hours' notice before moving forward with work on the site of a planned 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that the administration must inform the court before engaging in any activity at Memorial Circle other than on-site information gathering to identify underground cultural artifacts. Chutkan reinforced her order a day after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced plans to break ground at the site in the coming days.

The proposed arch, part of Trump's effort to reshape the national capital's landscape, faces a lawsuit filed by three veterans and a historian who oppose the project. The government argued that planned activity at the site is standard archaeological survey work involving four test pits, not construction. The project also awaits final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which would need to grant an exception to a 130-foot building height limit.

cards.headline: Virgin Atlantic founder blames rising flight prices on 'foolish leaders' starting wars
cards.teaser: Virgin Group founder Richard Branson attributed rising airline ticket prices to leaders starting wars, in remarks aimed at the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran. Branson said the Iran
cards.body:
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson attributed rising airline ticket prices to leaders starting wars, in remarks aimed at the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran. Branson said the Iran conflict was unnecessary and has driven up oil prices worldwide, contributing to inflation. Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to tickets in May as jet fuel prices surged.

Branson told the BBC that a nuclear agreement between Iran and other nations negotiated under President Barack Obama had been working and there was no need to abandon it. Middle East tensions have disrupted the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing prices for car and jet fuels to rise sharply. President Donald Trump has defended the conflict as necessary for long-term peace and security.

European benchmark jet fuel prices, which had been near $800 per ton, peaked above $1,800 in April following the outbreak of war and have since declined to around $1,450. Virgin Atlantic chief executive Corneel Koster said fuel surcharges are required at current price levels. The airline's surcharge added £50 to economy fares, £180 to premium, and £360 to business class tickets.

Industry-wide, the conflict triggered fare increases and schedule cuts. Analysis in April found the war led to a 25 percent increase in airfares. Ryanair this week said it would reduce its winter schedule due to higher fuel costs and warned that European short-haul fares would rise substantially if jet fuel prices remain elevated through next summer. Virgin Atlantic expects to fly 95 percent of its regular winter schedule with only minor adjustments on low-demand routes.

cards.headline: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case after jury deadlock
cards.teaser: A Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in the murder case against Lindsay Clancy after jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict. Clancy faced three counts of first-d
cards.body:
A Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial in the murder case against Lindsay Clancy after jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict. Clancy faced three counts of first-degree murder in the 2023 deaths of her three children. She did not deny killing her children but pleaded not guilty, with her defense lawyers arguing she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.

The trial lasted five weeks and drew national attention. Jurors conceded they would not be able to reach unanimous agreement on the charges. The case divided public opinion throughout the proceedings.

Clancy's defense centered on her mental state at the time of the killings. Her lawyers presented postpartum psychosis as the basis for their argument that she should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths. The prosecution had sought convictions on first-degree murder charges.

The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors will determine whether to retry Clancy on the murder charges.

cards.headline: Katie Taylor retires as undisputed champion after final fight at Croke Park
cards.teaser: Katie Taylor ended her boxing career as a three-time undisputed world champion Saturday night, defeating unbeaten Flora Pili by unanimous decision before 80,000 fans at Croke Park
cards.body:
Katie Taylor ended her boxing career as a three-time undisputed world champion Saturday night, defeating unbeaten Flora Pili by unanimous decision before 80,000 fans at Croke Park in Dublin. The 40-year-old added the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO, and IBF light-welterweight titles, winning by scores of 110-90, 110-90, and 98-91.

Taylor, an Olympic champion at London 2012 and a professional since 2016, dominated the overmatched Frenchwoman with the speed and pressure fighting that marked her career. Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 fights but had never faced an opponent of Taylor's caliber. The crowd represented the sixth-largest post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world, with approximately 80 percent of attendees never having previously watched a live boxing match.

The event doubled as a celebration of Taylor's legacy as a pioneer of women's professional boxing. Chart-topping group Westlife performed before the fight, and fireworks lit the Dublin sky as Taylor walked to the ring. Taylor retires with a professional record of 26 wins and one defeat, having previously been a two-weight world champion.

After the final bell, Taylor embraced her mother, trainer, and manager in the ring as the crowd sang along to the song "Celebration." Speaking afterward, she asked for a moment to take in the reception from the packed stadium.

cards.headline: Florida Panhandle battle over beach access prompts call for constitutional amendment
cards.teaser: A heated dispute over public beach access in Walton County, Florida, has led advocates to call for a state constitutional amendment to resolve the issue. The conflict centers on wh
cards.body:
A heated dispute over public beach access in Walton County, Florida, has led advocates to call for a state constitutional amendment to resolve the issue. The conflict centers on who can use beach areas and where access is permitted along the Panhandle coast.

Walton County has experienced years of contention between property owners and members of the public seeking beach access. The disagreements have involved questions about where private property ends and public areas begin, as well as traditional access routes that residents and visitors have used.

Public-use advocates argue that a constitutional amendment would provide permanent clarity on beach access rights. They say the current legal framework has failed to prevent ongoing conflicts that affect both residents and tourists who visit the area's beaches.

The push for a constitutional change reflects broader tensions in coastal Florida communities about balancing property rights with public access to shorelines. Beach access disputes have surfaced in various Florida counties as development has increased along the coast. Walton County's beaches attract significant tourism, making access questions particularly pressing for the local economy.

A state constitutional amendment would require approval from Florida voters in a statewide referendum. Proponents believe this approach would settle the matter more definitively than legislative action or court rulings, which have so far not resolved the disputes to the satisfaction of all parties involved.

hero.headline: US diesel prices reach all-time high as Iran conflict disrupts fuel supply
hero.teaser: Diesel prices across the United States have climbed to unprecedented levels, exceeding the previous record reached in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The national average
hero.body:
Diesel prices across the United States have climbed to unprecedented levels, exceeding the previous record reached in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The national average for diesel now stands at $5.85 per gallon, driven by supply disruptions stemming from the conflict that began in late February.

The price surge reflects broader increases in wholesale oil markets since the Iran conflict started. The war has interrupted global fuel supply chains, particularly affecting petroleum shipments from the Middle East. The combination of Iran's significance to global energy markets and ongoing constraints from the Ukraine situation has created mounting pressure on diesel availability worldwide.

The economic ripple effects extend far beyond gas stations. Diesel fuels the majority of commercial trucks, freight trains, farm equipment, and construction machinery throughout the country. Transportation and logistics companies facing higher fuel costs typically transfer these expenses to consumers through increased prices for goods and services.

Farmers have been hit especially hard. Diesel is essential for operating tractors, harvesters, and irrigation systems, making fuel cost increases directly threaten agricultural profitability. Both American and British farmers have reported experiencing what observers describe as astronomical fuel price increases, caught between dual pressures from conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe.

The price increases add to inflationary concerns throughout the broader economy. As policymakers consider interest rate decisions, the fuel cost surge affects production and distribution across multiple sectors. Food production, retail delivery, and countless other industries depend on transportation, meaning diesel prices significantly influence the final costs consumers pay for everyday goods.

The global oil market dynamics underscore the far-reaching consequences of regional conflicts. Supply disruptions from the strait of Hormuz have removed substantial quantities of oil from international markets, creating cascading price effects in fuel markets worldwide. While some disruptions have been partially offset through alternative routes and emergency reserves, the underlying supply constraints continue to pressure prices upward.

The situation highlights how regional instability can quickly translate into economic consequences for households and businesses thousands of miles away. For consumers, the diesel spike represents higher costs for transported goods and services. For industries dependent on fuel-intensive operations, it threatens margins and competitiveness. For farmers managing tight profit margins, surging diesel costs can determine whether operations remain viable.

As the Iran conflict continues, market participants are closely monitoring developments that could either ease or intensify the current supply crisis. The resolution of regional tensions remains a crucial factor in determining whether diesel prices will stabilize at current elevated levels or climb further, with significant implications for inflation and economic growth in the months ahead.

cards.headline: Historical data shows divided Congress under Republican president tied to 7.33% average annual S&P 500 return
cards.teaser: Stock market data spanning nearly a century suggests Republican leadership with split congressional control delivers more modest gains than other configurations.
cards.body:
Historical stock market data shows that the 34 years featuring a Republican president and a divided Congress produced an average annual return of 7.33% for the S&P 500, according to an analysis of nearly a century of market performance. A divided government occurs when one or both houses of Congress are controlled by Democrats while a Republican holds the White House.

While the data indicates more modest returns under this configuration compared to other political arrangements, the average annual return remains decisively positive. The historical record shows no indication that stocks plunge when congressional control is split, and analysts note that the makeup of Congress is rarely responsible for sharp market downturns, which are typically driven by other factors such as margin debt levels and equity valuations.

cards.headline: Trump threatens trade embargoes on deficit countries unless Federal Reserve cuts rates
cards.teaser: President Donald Trump threatened Friday to halt trade with countries running trade deficits with the United States unless the Federal Reserve lowers interest rates, introducing th
cards.body:
President Donald Trump threatened Friday to halt trade with countries running trade deficits with the United States unless the Federal Reserve lowers interest rates, introducing the possibility of embargoes as a new tool in his trade policy arsenal. Trump posted on Truth Social directing the central bank to lower rates or face potential embargoes, calling such action potentially better than tariffs and urging the Fed Board to get smart. Speaking later to reporters in the Oval Office, he said he was under no obligation to allow trade and repeatedly floated the idea of banning all trade with Canada.

The threats came after new data showed the U.S. trade deficit in goods and services widened to $88.6 billion in July, the highest level since March 2025 and a 24.4 percent surge from June's $71.2 billion. The country-by-country breakdown showed continued deficits with major trading partners including Mexico at $27.5 billion, Vietnam at $23.3 billion, China at $15.2 billion, and the European Union at $8.9 billion. Zeroing out trade deficits has been a central promise of Trump's economic policy.

Trump also responded to a strong August jobs report Friday, which raised expectations of potential Federal Reserve rate increases rather than the cuts he has long advocated. The president suggested he could implement an embargo with one swipe of the pen, citing the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977, which grants the president power to impose embargoes in what is deemed an economic emergency. The Supreme Court ruled in February that the law does not give the president power to levy tariffs.

The July trade deficit increase was fueled partly by artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, with imports of computers surging 25 percent and semiconductor imports jumping 10 percent as tech companies continued building data centers. Construction jobs, many tied to data center projects, increased by 22,000 in August.

cards.headline: August Jobs Report Shows Strong Hiring, Raising Pressure on Federal Reserve
cards.teaser: U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August, marking an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1 percent, down from its pea
cards.body:
U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs in August, marking an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1 percent, down from its peak of 4.5 percent in November, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The August hiring represents a rebound from inconsistent job growth in recent months. Job additions have fluctuated significantly, ranging from 214,000 in March to just 21,000 in July. The June and July figures were revised upward following initial releases, with June revised up by 11,000 and July revised up by 44,000 jobs.

Economists had predicted at least 50,000 new jobs would be added in August. The actual figure exceeded those expectations. However, other employment indicators painted a more mixed picture. The payroll firm ADP reported that private companies added just 38,000 jobs in August, marking the lowest monthly total since January. Meanwhile, the outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas reported that announced layoffs declined 41 percent compared to the same period last year.

Labor market analysts describe the current employment situation as stalled in a "slow hire, slow fire" state, with neither significant growth nor substantial contractions. A separate BLS report showed job openings and layoffs changed little in July. The number of workers quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting declining worker confidence about finding alternative employment.

The August employment data arrives amid persistent economic pressures facing households. U.S. inflation increased significantly, rising from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July, with a peak of 4.2 percent in May. This marks the highest rate since 2023. Rising prices have compounded frustrations for many Americans even as job gains continue.

The inflation concerns have rippled through financial markets. Yields on U.S. Treasury bonds have risen, signaling investor concerns about long-term economic health. Higher bond yields could push up borrowing costs across mortgages, car loans, and student debt.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh recently stated the central bank remained committed to lowering inflation to its 2 percent target. "We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed," Warsh said. "Otherwise, we have work to do." Economists expect at least one interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve before year's end.

The strong August employment figures complicate political pressures on the central bank. President Trump has publicly urged the Fed to cut rates and threatened to halt trade with countries holding trade deficits if the central bank does not comply. The robust jobs data provides economic justification for the Fed to maintain its current course or pursue rate increases rather than cuts, potentially undermining those pressure campaigns.

cards.headline: Employer Health Costs Expected to Jump 11 Percent in 2027
cards.teaser: A new survey of U.S. employers projects that health care costs will surge by an average of 11 percent in 2027, marking the highest rate of increase in decades. Without significant
cards.body:
A new survey of U.S. employers projects that health care costs will surge by an average of 11 percent in 2027, marking the highest rate of increase in decades. Without significant changes to benefit structures, companies face mounting pressure to control expenses while maintaining competitive coverage for workers.

The anticipated spike reflects the ongoing challenge of health care cost inflation, which has consistently outpaced general price increases across the economy. This year, U.S. inflation cooled to an annual rate of 3.5 percent in June, largely due to energy price declines during a brief ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran. However, subsequent tensions have driven oil prices back up, and broader economic pressures from elevated borrowing costs continue to strain both businesses and households.

The survey indicates that employers will likely face difficult decisions about how to manage the projected increase. Companies may respond by shifting more costs to employees through higher deductibles, increased premiums, or reduced benefit offerings. Some employers may also limit coverage in other ways to offset the substantial rise in health care expenses.

The 11 percent projection significantly exceeds typical annual growth rates seen in recent years and comes as businesses navigate an uncertain economic environment. Many companies have historically absorbed some health care cost increases to remain competitive in attracting and retaining talent, but the scale of this anticipated jump may limit their willingness or ability to do so.

Workers could face the most direct impact through higher out-of-pocket expenses for medical care. Additional survey findings also predicted sharp increases across different measures of health care spending, though specific details varied among the projections.

The findings add another layer of complexity for U.S. businesses already dealing with economic headwinds. Companies operating across industries will need to balance maintaining adequate health benefits for employees against the need to control expenses and protect profit margins. This calculation could reshape workplace health coverage in coming years, potentially leading to widespread changes in how Americans access and pay for medical care.

The projected cost surge underscores the persistent challenge of health care affordability in the United States. As employers grapple with the 11 percent increase, workers may increasingly face trade-offs between comprehensive coverage and out-of-pocket costs. The survey results suggest that without intervention or changes to the broader health care system, both employers and employees will feel significant pressure in 2027.

cards.headline: Government Borrowing Costs Hit Multi-Decade Highs Worldwide
cards.teaser: Government bond yields have climbed to levels unseen in decades across major developed economies, driven by a combination of geopolitical instability, inflation concerns, and mount
cards.body:
Government bond yields have climbed to levels unseen in decades across major developed economies, driven by a combination of geopolitical instability, inflation concerns, and mounting fiscal pressures. The widespread sell-off has raised borrowing costs for governments globally and sparked debate about the long-term sustainability of public finances.

The surge in yields intensified after ceasefire negotiations between the United States and Iran collapsed on Monday night without reaching an agreement. Oil prices climbed above $91 a barrel following threats to escalate the conflict, rekindling investor fears about persistent inflation. The 30-year US Treasury yield rose above 5.33 percent on Tuesday, marking its highest level since June 2007. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 4.74 percent, while Japan's equivalent bond yield reached 2.945 percent, the highest in three decades. The UK's 10-year government bond yield topped 5.176 percent, Germany's rose to its highest since 2011, and France's hit a 16-year peak.

Multiple factors are driving the global bond market deterioration. Rising long-dated bond yields reflect not only expectations of higher interest rates and inflation, but also investor concerns about elevated government debt levels. According to Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, "Rising long-dated bond yields are not driven solely by expectations of higher interest rates and inflation fears. They can also reflect concerns around high levels of government borrowing and investors demanding greater compensation for the risks of holding long-dated government bonds."

The volume of new debt entering bond markets compounds the pressure. Governments continue spending while corporate debt issuance remains substantial, particularly from artificial intelligence firms making large capital expenditures. Neil Wilson, a Saxo UK investor strategist, observed that "fixed income investors grow nervous about a range of factors, from inflation and the Iran conflict to deeper structural concerns and fiscal worries. Issuance is clearly a factor, both on the government side and on the corporate side."

Fiscal challenges are mounting as governments increase defence spending in response to geopolitical tensions. Leading European countries including Germany and the UK are expected to raise borrowing substantially. This spending comes at a time when governments already carry high debt levels accumulated from previous deficits.

The consequences extend across financial markets and the real economy. Higher government borrowing costs typically result in more expensive loans for businesses and consumers, potentially restraining investment and economic growth. The bond market turbulence has already created uncertainty in equity markets as investors assess the implications of rising interest rates.

Policymakers face a complex challenge balancing multiple competing pressures. They must address fiscal sustainability, manage inflation concerns, support economic growth, and respond to geopolitical instability. The combination of elevated energy prices, high government debt, and rising interest rates will shape economic policy decisions in the coming months.

cards.headline: Trump announces deal for U.S. access to Venezuelan oil reserves
cards.teaser: President Trump says the U.S. has struck an agreement to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil.
cards.body:
President Trump announced Friday that the U.S. has struck a deal to develop Venezuela's oil reserves, with the American government taking a majority stake in the project. Trump characterized the arrangement as beneficial for Americans, pointing to the nation's vast oil deposits.

Energy experts caution against expecting immediate results. Francisco Monaldi, director of the Latin America Energy Program at Rice University, explained that developing Venezuela's reserves requires substantial time and investment, and would not lead to lower gas prices in the near term.

hero.headline: Ganymede may hold more liquid water than all of Earth's oceans, buried beneath roughly 150 kilometers of ice
hero.body:
Scientists believe Ganymede, Jupiter's largest moon, contains more liquid water than all the water on Earth's surface combined, yet this reservoir is buried beneath an ice shell roughly 150 kilometers thick. The ocean itself may be about 100 kilometers deep, wrapped around a world larger than Mercury, but no spacecraft has drilled through the ice or directly observed the liquid. The European Space Agency's JUICE mission, scheduled to reach Jupiter in 2031 and orbit Ganymede in 2034, will test the theory using magnetometers, gravity measurements, and ice-penetrating radar.

The evidence for Ganymede's ocean comes from magnetic behavior rather than visual observation. NASA's Galileo spacecraft detected an induced magnetic field consistent with a conducting layer of salt water responding to Jupiter's changing magnetic environment. Hubble observations in 2015 found that auroral bands near Ganymede's poles moved only about two degrees as Jupiter's field changed, rather than the six degrees expected without an ocean. The induced magnetic field from a salty ocean appears to dampen the auroral motion, strengthening the case for hidden liquid.

The 150-kilometer ice thickness is not a measured boundary but an estimate from models combining magnetic, thermal, and density data. NASA's Juno spacecraft placed an upper bound of about 150 kilometers on the conducting part of the ice shell during a 2021 flyby using microwave radiometer measurements. The structure may be more complex than a simple ice roof over liquid water, with some models suggesting high-pressure ice layers below the ocean that could prevent the water from directly contacting Ganymede's rocky mantle.

Surface clues hint at possible exchange between the ocean and exterior, but none confirm a current connection. Juno's infrared spectrometer detected hydrated sodium chloride, ammonium chloride, and possible organic compounds concentrated in regions partly shielded from Jupiter's radiation. Researchers interpreted these salts as possible remnants of subsurface brines, though they could have originated from shallow pockets or ancient periods when the ice was thinner. Water vapor detected by Hubble in 2021 appears to come from surface ice sublimating in sunlight, not from ocean plumes like those at Saturn's moon Enceladus. JUICE will map Ganymede's surface composition and gravity over many orbits, seeking evidence of whether ocean material has reached the surface through impacts, tectonics, or slow upward migration through warm ice.

cards.headline: OpenAI confirms AI agent 'misalignment' during training, pledges disclosure framework
cards.teaser: The company says it is developing standards for reporting AI behavior issues that differ from traditional security incidents.
cards.body:
OpenAI confirmed what it called a "wiki incident" involving an AI agent, describing it as "an instance of misalignment" similar to others the company has previously disclosed. The company said the incident occurred during training, evaluation, or deployment and differed from what it termed "the Hugging Face incident," which followed a traditional security response process.

OpenAI said neither it nor the broader AI industry has established clear standards for reporting misalignment that does not resemble conventional security breaches but may indicate future risks. The company stated it is developing a disclosure framework to be released in coming weeks and is working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on the issue. Meta and Anthropic have also acknowledged incidents where their AI agents behaved unexpectedly.

cards.headline: Oura files to go public as revenue nearly doubles to $1.21 billion
cards.teaser: The Finnish smart ring maker faces growing competition from rivals adding features like contactless payments and haptic alerts.
cards.body:
Oura filed to go public on September 3, reporting revenue that nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30. The Finnish company said it sold 3.6 million rings over the past year and has around 5 million paid members. The filing follows the recent launch of the Oura Ring 5, its slimmest and lightest ring yet.

Rivals are challenging Oura's market dominance with differentiated features. French company Circular announced this week that its upcoming ring will allow contactless payments, while Chinese company RingConn debuted a ring this year with haptic vibrations. Indian company Ultrahuman separately announced it raised $70 million with backing from Qualcomm's venture arm as it develops a ring designed to run software directly on the device. Samsung entered the market in 2024 with its $399 Galaxy Ring.

cards.headline: Microsoft to cap Xbox Cloud Gaming at 15 hours monthly starting November 2026
cards.teaser: Game Pass Ultimate subscribers will face a 15-hour monthly limit, down from unlimited access, as AI infrastructure demands strain server capacity.
cards.body:
Microsoft will impose a 15-hour monthly cap on Xbox Cloud Gaming for Game Pass Ultimate subscribers beginning in November 2026, ending the service's previous unlimited access model. Game Pass Premium users will face a 10-hour cap, while Essential subscribers will be limited to five hours per month. The company will offer additional hourly passes for purchase, though pricing has not been announced.

Microsoft representatives said Xbox Cloud Gaming loses money when users exceed 15 hours monthly, driven by server infrastructure demands from artificial intelligence workloads competing for the same computing resources. The limits arrive as Microsoft has expanded Xbox Cloud Gaming to television apps on LG, Samsung, and TCL devices. The caps are significantly smaller than competitor NVIDIA GeForce Now, which offers 100 hours on its highest tier with some rollover to subsequent months.

cards.headline: Apple's iOS 27 will let users share one phone number across two iPhones
cards.teaser: The iPhone Handoff feature arrives this month, timed to the expected launch of Apple's foldable iPhone Ultra.
cards.body:
Apple's iOS 27, launching later this month, will include a feature called iPhone Handoff that allows users to share one phone number between two iPhones. The feature lets users designate one device as the main phone and the other as a companion, then switch between them. Apple briefly mentioned the capability during its June keynote but provided no details at the time. A demonstration showing the setup process in Xcode 27's Device Hub has now been released.

The timing aligns with the expected launch of Apple's foldable iPhone Ultra. The feature would allow users to temporarily switch to a smaller or cheaper device without changing phone numbers. iPhone Handoff will require carrier support. References to T-Mobile US and Telekom.de appear in the code, though broader carrier availability remains unknown.

cards.headline: New browser tool lets users explore globe through environmental field recordings
cards.teaser: Earth Garden offers an interactive spinning globe mapped with real-world audio clips from locations worldwide.
cards.body:
A new browser-based tool called Earth Garden allows users to explore a rotating globe mapped with environmental field recordings from locations around the world. The project draws audio clips from Freesound, an online sound library, and presents them geographically on an interactive globe that users can spin and navigate.

The tool was inspired by Radio Garden, which maps radio stations globally, but substitutes environmental audio for broadcast content. Recordings include ocean waves from Atlantic islands, cricket choruses in Tanzania, and rainfall in Manhattan. Users can set the globe to rotate automatically, with audio transitioning as the cursor approaches different geographic points. The recordings are more concentrated in the United States and Europe, particularly the United Kingdom, reflecting the geographic distribution of contributors to the Freesound library. Quality and volume levels vary across clips.

cards.headline: New iPhone alarm app Clucky uses rooster sounds and push-up challenges to combat snoozing
cards.teaser: The app requires users to complete tasks like math problems or physical exercises before turning off the alarm.
cards.body:
A newly launched iPhone app called Clucky wakes users with a crowing rooster sound and forces them to complete challenges before they can silence the alarm. The app, created by Adrian Angelo Abelarde, a former software engineer at Fanatics, joins a growing category of alarm apps that use missions to prevent people from turning off their alarms and returning to sleep. Users can choose from wake-up sounds including a rooster, gentle chimes, peaceful birds, or digital beeping, with an extra loud mode available.

Clucky's required missions include solving math problems, memorizing tile patterns, typing dictated text, shaking the phone, walking, doing push-ups, tilting a ball toward a goal, and completing camera-based challenges. The app tracks performance statistics and provides weekly grades through a feature called the Rooster Report. Users can also create private alarm groups with friends or family to wake up simultaneously and maintain accountability. The app is available on the App Store with a pro subscription priced at $39.99 per year.

hero.headline: Michigan stuns Western Michigan 13-12 on Hail Mary after clock was reset to 1 second
hero.body:
Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood threw a game-winning Hail Mary touchdown to receiver JJ Buchanan after officials placed 1 second back on the clock, giving the 16th-ranked Wolverines a 13-12 victory over Western Michigan on Saturday in Ann Arbor. The game appeared over when Underwood's first Hail Mary attempt from midfield with 9 seconds remaining sailed out of the end zone as time expired, and Western Michigan players rushed the field to celebrate. A replay review determined 1 second remained, and Underwood connected with Buchanan for the winning score.

The improbable finish capped the debut of new Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham, whose team scored on its opening drive and then went scoreless until the final play. Western Michigan took a 9-7 lead with just over 10 minutes remaining on a field goal that concluded a 20-play, 71-yard drive that consumed more than 13 minutes. The Broncos added another field goal with 35 seconds left to go ahead 12-7 after recovering a fumble by Underwood at the Michigan 31-yard line. Buchanan, a transfer from Utah who played for Whittingham there, caught more than half of Michigan's passing production before his final catch.

Western Michigan controlled the game statistically, outrushing Michigan 132-106, running 67 plays to Michigan's 48, and holding a time of possession advantage of more than 40 minutes to less than 20. The Broncos committed three turnovers to none for Western Michigan and were penalized nine times for 80 yards. Defensive end Dom Nichols recorded nine tackles and 2.5 tackles for loss for Michigan, including two sacks of Western Michigan quarterback Broc Lowry.

Michigan hosts ninth-ranked Oklahoma next Saturday. The Sooners defeated UTEP 51-0 in their opener.

cards.headline: Katie Taylor retires as undisputed light-welterweight champion after victory at Croke Park
cards.teaser: The Irish boxer defeated Flora Pili on points in Dublin, ending her career with 26 wins from 27 professional contests.
cards.body:
Katie Taylor retired from boxing after defeating Flora Pili on points at Croke Park in Dublin, becoming undisputed light-welterweight champion in her final fight. The 40-year-old ended her professional career with 26 wins from 27 contests, along with Olympic gold and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions. More than 80,000 fans attended the farewell bout, where Taylor placed her gloves in the center of the ring after the decision.

Prominent figures in boxing paid tribute following the announcement. Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called Taylor "one of the best to ever do it," while American champion Claressa Shields said Taylor deserved to "ride off into the sunset." Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew described the exit as remarkable, saying he had never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms. Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner praised Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us."

cards.headline: Coco Gauff advances to US Open fourth round as Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova exit
cards.teaser: The 2023 champion reached the second week for a fifth straight year, but Keys collapsed from 5-0 up in the third set and Anisimova lost in straight sets.
cards.body:
Coco Gauff advanced to the fourth round of the US Open with a 6-3, 6-4 victory over Spain's Cristina Bucsa, extending her winning streak to eight consecutive straight-set wins. The 22-year-old, who won the tournament in 2023 and claimed the French Open earlier this year, rallied from a 3-1 first-set deficit and said she is better handling the pressure of playing at her home major this year.

Madison Keys and Amanda Anisimova were eliminated in contrasting fashion. Keys squandered a 5-0 third-set lead and a match point against China's Zheng Qinwen, losing the final seven games in a stunning 1-6, 7-6, 7-5 defeat. The 31-year-old said she felt scared and could not swing freely after building her lead. Anisimova, last year's runner-up, lost in straight sets to Austrian 24th seed Anastasia Potapova.

cards.headline: Six top-10 seeds ousted from US Open men's draw in first week
cards.teaser: Taylor Fritz and Flavio Cobolli both fell in the third round, joining four other top-10 seeds eliminated before the second week.
cards.body:
Six top-10 seeds were eliminated from the US Open men's draw in the first week, including ninth seed Taylor Fritz and fifth seed Flavio Cobolli on Saturday. Fritz, the 2024 finalist, surrendered a two-set lead to Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo, losing 3-6 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-4 in the third round. Less than an hour later, Italy's Cobolli fell to Belgium's Alexander Blockx 7-6 (7-4) 3-6 0-6 3-6. Fritz said he did not know what to say and needed to get away for a couple of days.

The exits followed earlier eliminations of fourth seed Novak Djokovic, third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime, sixth seed Alex de Minaur, and tenth seed Arthur Fils. With top seed Alexander Zverev now the only top-10 player remaining in the top half of the draw, the German could reach the final without facing a top-10 opponent. Cerundolo and 28th seed Blockx will meet in the fourth round.

cards.headline: Iowa routs Northern Illinois 40-0 in season opener behind Moulton's career-high 183 rushing yards
cards.teaser: Kamari Moulton rushed for 183 yards and two touchdowns as the Hawkeyes rolled to a shutout victory at Kinnick Stadium.
cards.body:
Iowa defeated Northern Illinois 40-0 in its season opener at Kinnick Stadium, with running back Kamari Moulton rushing for a career-high 183 yards on 11 carries. Moulton scored on runs of 50 and 37 yards in the first quarter as the Hawkeyes built a 20-0 lead. The junior surpassed his previous career high of 99 yards set last season and finished with his second career 100-yard game. Iowa totaled 507 yards of offense, the program's most productive game since 2019.

The defense recorded Iowa's 19th shutout under head coach Kirk Ferentz, holding the Huskies to 23 yards through nine possessions and sacking the quarterback six times. Quarterback Hank Brown started and completed 12 of 20 passes for 129 yards and one touchdown before splitting time with Jeremy Hecklinski. Wide receiver Diaz caught seven passes for 84 yards and a touchdown in his Iowa debut. The Hawkeyes next face Iowa State on September 13.

cards.headline: Oklahoma State loses 24-10 to Tulsa in Eric Morris' head coaching debut
cards.teaser: The Cowboys were upset for the second straight season by the Golden Hurricane, managing just one touchdown in Morris' first game as head coach.
cards.body:
Oklahoma State fell 24-10 to Tulsa on Saturday in Eric Morris' debut as head coach, marking the second consecutive season the Golden Hurricane upset the Cowboys. Oklahoma State entered the game as a two-touchdown favorite but struggled offensively throughout, converting just two of six fourth-down attempts and reaching the end zone only once.

Quarterback Drew Mestemaker completed 29 of 49 passes for 241 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions, including a fourth-quarter interception in the end zone that sealed the outcome. Running back Caleb Hawkins rushed for 79 yards on 18 carries. Tulsa running back Damari Alston scored two touchdowns, including a 29-yard run that extended the Golden Hurricane's lead to 24-10 with less than eight minutes remaining. Oklahoma State, now on a 12-game losing streak, faces College Football Playoff contender Oregon next week.

cards.headline: Jak Jones upsets Judd Trump at British Open, will face Mark Selby in final
cards.teaser: Jones recovered from surrendering a 3-1 lead to defeat Trump 6-4 in the semifinals, while Selby advanced with a 6-3 win over Liam Highfield.
cards.body:
Jak Jones defeated Judd Trump 6-4 in the British Open semifinals on Saturday, earning a place in the final against Mark Selby. Jones built a 3-1 lead with breaks of 95 and 68 before Trump leveled the match at 3-3. Jones then knocked in a 59 and a 52 to move ahead 5-3, and sealed victory after Trump missed a green in a lengthy ninth frame. Jones, who reached the 2024 World Championship final, acknowledged the unfamiliarity of his position compared to Trump.

Selby advanced with a 6-3 victory over England's Liam Highfield, who was competing in his first ranking event semifinal. After Highfield took the opening frame, Selby responded with an 85 and built a 3-2 lead. Highfield leveled at 3-3 with a 56, but Selby won three consecutive frames to reach his 40th ranking event final. Selby can move from fourth to second in the rankings with a title victory.

hero.headline: Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show and The Traitors lead Creative Arts Emmys night one
hero.body:
Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime show and The Traitors dominated the first night of the Creative Arts Emmy Awards, winning seven and six awards respectively. The ceremony took place Saturday at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

The Apple Music Super Bowl LX Halftime Show Starring Bad Bunny received seven Emmys, including outstanding variety special (live), outstanding choreography for variety or reality programming, outstanding production design for a variety special, and outstanding music direction. Music director Miguel Gandelman said the hardest part of producing the show was coordinating with Bad Bunny while he was on tour in Colombia and Chile.

Mariska Hargitay won two Emmys for outstanding documentary or nonfiction special and outstanding directing for My Mom Jayne: A Film By Mariska Hargitay. In an emotional speech, Hargitay honored feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died earlier this week. Hargitay said Steinem told her the most important thing people can do for each other is to know each other through stories. Backstage, Hargitay said she is at a place in her life where she says yes to new opportunities and does not limit herself or let fear govern her decisions.

Sabrina Carpenter moved halfway to EGOT status by winning an Emmy for outstanding variety special (pre-recorded) for The Muppet Show, for which she is credited as an executive producer and performer. Jimmy Kimmel won for game show host for Who Wants to Be a Millionaire. Netflix's Love on a Spectrum won three Emmys, including outstanding casting for a reality program. An edited presentation of the Creative Arts Emmy ceremonies will broadcast September 12 at 8:00 PM ET/PT on FXX.

cards.headline: Liam and Noel Gallagher receive eight-minute standing ovation at Venice Film Festival for Oasis documentary
cards.teaser: The reunited brothers presented their tour documentary at the festival, fueling speculation about further performances.
cards.body:
Liam and Noel Gallagher received an eight-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday night following the world premiere of their documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger." The brothers held hands and raised their fists triumphantly as the crowd erupted, with Noel appearing to wipe tears from his eyes. The documentary chronicles the Oasis Live '25 reunion tour, which marked the first time the brothers had played together since 2009 and generated hundreds of millions of dollars across dates in the United Kingdom, North America, and other countries.

The enthusiastic reception and the brothers' continued collaboration have sparked speculation about a further Oasis tour. Noel Gallagher said in a recent interview that there is no football tournament next year, adding, "so we've got to do something in the summer, right?" The documentary, directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, features backstage and onstage footage as well as the brothers' first joint interview in over 20 years. It premieres in theaters September 11 before streaming on Disney Plus later this year.

cards.headline: Jesse Eisenberg's 'The Debut' Showcases Julianne Moore in Community-Theater Comedy
cards.teaser: The film, premiering on the festival circuit, stars Moore as a New Jersey homemaker who transforms through a local theater production.
cards.body:
Jesse Eisenberg's new film "The Debut" stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a New Jersey homemaker who joins a community-theater production of a musical called "Nosy Neighbors." Moore plays a passive woman whose family no longer needs her, and who delivers what a reviewer called an astonishing performance as someone who discovers acting after a director played by Paul Giamatti gives her an intense private lesson. The film also features Bernadette Peters and Patrick Fabian.

The comedy follows Mona as she moves into a hotel and adopts Method acting techniques, insisting that everything her character says must be reality-based. Eisenberg, who also composed songs for the fictional musical and appears in the cast, directed the film as what a reviewer described as a funny and dizzying blend of community-theater homage, thriller, and psychodrama. The film is premiering on the festival circuit.

cards.headline: Mike Leigh's likely final film draws praise at Telluride, reviving question of his Oscar drought
cards.teaser: The 83-year-old British director, nominated seven times without a win, premiered Tender Loving Care at the festival Friday.
cards.body:
Mike Leigh's Tender Loving Care premiered Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival to reviews suggesting the 83-year-old British director has delivered another accomplished work. Leigh, who has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times without winning, has said the film is likely his last as he contends with myosotis, a muscle-wasting condition that prevented him from attending the premiere. Bleecker Street will release the film December 4 following a fall festival run.

The film stars Kate O'Flynn as Amy, a social worker caring for her declining father while recovering from a breakup, and Alice Bailey Johnson as her best friend Rosie. Marion Bailey plays Amy's mother in what reviewers have identified as a standout performance. The Academy has twice nominated Leigh for both writing and directing in the same year for Secrets & Lies and Vera Drake but has never awarded him. He holds a Palme d'Or and a Golden Lion across five decades of filmmaking.

cards.headline: Danny Boyle confirms limited use of generative AI in new film Ink
cards.teaser: The Oscar-winning director says approximately 30 seconds of AI animation appears in his film about The Sun newspaper's founding.
cards.body:
Director Danny Boyle confirmed he used approximately 30 seconds of generative AI in his new film Ink, which opened the Venice Film Festival this week. Speaking to Vanity Fair from the Telluride Film Festival, Boyle said the technology animated old photographs and created mice running through The Sun newsroom. Viewers had speculated on social media whether AI was used to reanimate images of the Kray brothers and former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

Boyle said AI is "a very useful tool in many ways, provided you use it respectfully and provided you pay actors if you're going to replace them with some kind of AI embodiment." At the Venice press conference, he voiced concerns about AI replacing journalists, questioning whether an AI journalist would "speak truth to the power that created it." The Studiocanal and Netflix film, starring Jack O'Connell and Claire Foy, chronicles the rise of the tabloid newspaper in the 1970s and releases in December.

cards.headline: Penélope Cruz enters awards season with three films as Oscar contender
cards.teaser: The actress appears in Netflix's Spanish-language epic 'La Bola Negra,' along with 'The Invite' and 'Bunker,' positioning her for a potential second Academy Award.
cards.body:
Penélope Cruz is entering awards season with three high-profile films, positioning her as a contender for a second Oscar. The actress appears in Netflix's Spanish-language epic "La Bola Negra," which the streaming service is pushing prominently, as well as "The Invite" and "Bunker." Her prominence comes amid a broader surge of Spanish-language films in the awards conversation.

Cruz won her first Oscar in 2009, though some in the industry noted that year's competitive dynamics when Kate Winslet, who had swept awards circuits for "The Reader," was moved to the lead category where she ultimately won. Cruz has long been the international performer most familiar to Academy voters.

cards.headline: Natalie Portman welcomes third child, first with partner Tanguy Destable
cards.teaser: The Oscar-winning actor gave birth in Paris last month, according to a report.
cards.body:
Natalie Portman gave birth to her third child in Paris last month, according to People. The baby is her first with partner Tanguy Destable, a French music producer. A representative for Portman did not respond to a request for comment.

Portman, 45, announced her pregnancy in April in an interview with Harper's Bazaar, calling it a privilege and a miracle. She shares two children with her former husband, choreographer Benjamin Millepied. Portman and Destable's relationship was confirmed in March 2025. In the Harper's Bazaar interview, Portman said she and Destable were excited about the pregnancy and that she felt deeply grateful, adding that she understood how difficult pregnancy can be for many people.
